newsitem.title: UK: Unbalanced UK economy poses serious inflation risk.
newsitem.headline: Unbalanced UK economy poses serious inflation risk.

text.p: The imbalance in the British economy between lively services sector growth and still sluggish manufacturing output carries a serious risk for inflation, economists said.
"This imbalance has serious implications for inflation," said Neil Blake, research director at Business Strategies Ltd.

"Investment in services tends to be very lumpy -- much more so than manufacturing -- so it is easy to run into capacity contraints, and the sector also enjoys a lack of competition from imports, unlike manufacturing."

Latest GDP data showed the economic growth accelerated to 1.0 percent in the first quarter, up from 0.8 percent in the fourth. Year-on-year growth picked up to 3.0 percent compared with 2.6 percent in the fourth. The breakdown showed the recovery is still being driven by the services industry, with output up 1.2 percent for year-on-year growth of 3.9 percent.
Inflationary pressures are already building in the services sector.

Labour market data this year has clearly shown wage pressures building there, and the latest British Chambers of Commerce survey said two-thirds of service sector firms experienced recrutiment difficulties in the first quarter.
"Prices and wages pressure are already more intense in the services sector. That has reinforced our view that interest rates need to rise," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.

But economists are aware that an interest rate rise, widely expected soon after the May 1 election, may punish manufacturers more than service sector firms. "It's difficult to know in advance how monetary tightening will affect the two sectors," said Blake.

Its effect on manufacturing really depends on how the pound reacts. The pound has appreciated by 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August, driven higher on expectations of higher interest rates. Another rate rise could send it even higher, although there is a chance when interest rate expectations are realised the rally will correct.
The impact of a rate rise on the services sector depends largely on how consumers respond -- to what extent mortgage payments eat into their disposable income, said Blake.
"The obvious thing for the next government to do is to be wary of a rate rise and look instead for personal tax rises."

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC agreed. He said the pace of overall growth will increase calls for policy action to prevent overheating. "But sharp rises in interest rates would threaten to further unbalance growth by tipping industry back into recession. A fiscal tighening would appear to be the correct policy prescription."
